To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the s dependence of hadron multiplicities and transverse momenta is well described by all models, (ii) the s dependence for the mean charged multiplicity is well described by sibyll and qgsjet, (iii) the s dependence is poorly described for the mean neutral multiplicity by all models, and (iv) the s dependence on the mean charged multiparticle pseudorapidity density is well described only by sibyll, while the others are in reasonable agreement

(1) the LHC proton–proton data are consistent with the predictions of the hadronic models used in the cosmic ray field; (2) there is a large spread in predictions of the various models; (3) there is no single model that is able to simultaneously describe the LHC data and the cosmic-ray data at the highest energies; (4) the Lhc data provide a new constraint on the hadronic models, which is complementary to the one provided

(i) none of the hadronic MC models used in CR physics is able to reproduce the full range of the LHC data, and that (ii) this is not due to the lack of high-energy data, but rather to the fact that the models have been tuned to the data at lower energies, where the LHC measurements are not available, and are therefore unable to describe the LHC data at the higher energy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the properties of the fundamental interactions of nature, in the framework of the Standard Model and beyond.
the development and application of methods for the analysis of data from the Pierre Auger Observatory.
the development of a new generation of hadronic interaction models for ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray physics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LHC data have not yet provided a clear and decisive answer on the question of which model is the best one for UHECR physics, but that they have certainly provided valuable new information that will be useful for future studies.
the current generation of hadronic models used in cosmic-ray physics are in reasonable agreement with LHC measurements
, while the overall agreement is good, there are still significant deviations in the details of the data–theory comparisons, and the LHC results are a clear challenge to the hadronic models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LHC data are consistent with the predictions of all models considered here.
the first LHC results do not provide any strong indication of the superiority of any one of the hadronic models, but they do provide some useful guidance for future improvements of the models.
the first LHC proton–proton data have already significantly constrained the predictions for the hadronic interaction models used commonly in CR physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the new LHC results have the potential of significantly improving the accuracy of UHECR measurements.

the new LHC proton–proton data provide an important tool for constraining models used in CR physics, and that the LHC data are already starting to provide useful information for the modeling of CR interactions.
the new LHC results have already put constraints on the modeling of hadronic interactions in the energy range 10–1000 TeV.
